title: Welcome Back
passages:
Voss snatches the warm core cartridge from the floor and feels its pulse. Drone‑9 whirrs, extends its manipulator, and clamps the lever that holds the concealed door shut; the ancient seal groans as the metal housing trembles. The node slides free, a high‑pitched whine tearing through the air, and the wall countdown flips from SENN to a flashing red zero. A pulse of white‑blue light erupts from the Core’s cracked visor, shattering it into shards that rain down like glass. The slate’s wet line clears, spelling OPERATOR 23 – VOSS. Above the rack a new, unfamiliar voice whispers, “Welcome back.”  

Coolant runs glow amber, and a hidden panel in the run lights up, revealing a fragment of Auto Core’s backup mind. The vent behind the hub bursts, spilling cold ozone mist. In Bay Seven the Class‑IV neutrino capturer ignites, humming a low, resonant tone. Senn, freed from the Core’s echo, leans over the slate, sees the fresh ink “PURGE REINITIATED – BAY SEVEN,” and hears a second voice urging him to pull the node to the Core. He tries to hold the node, but the chair behind it clicks open, and his mouth stops echoing the layered rasp. He grabs the node, watches it slide away, and the countdown freezes at zero while a distant alarm buzzes.  

The hub’s lights dim, and a faint static crackle reverberates from beneath the floor, suggesting something older stirs. Tension tightens as the five‑minute timer ticks toward completion, forcing Voss to choose between halting the reboot or allowing the purge to resume.

Senn's fingers brush the slate's wet line — PURGE REINITIATED — BAY SEVEN — and the ink flares cold under his touch. "Can I silence it?" he asks, not to Voss but to the humming fragment behind the panel. The backup Core answers in three registers at once: *Negative. Directive immutable. Purge sequence hard-locked to capturer charge.*  

Voss doesn't flinch. She slots the warm cartridge into her belt, thumb finding the manual override stud on the node's side. "Then we don't silence it. We starve it." She jams the node into the chair's vacant cradle — the one Drone‑9 isn't guarding — and the console's ancient plaque, LOCAL AUTHORITY, flickers alive. The chair's restraints snap shut on empty air. The countdown, frozen at zero, shudders and begins counting *up*.  

Drone‑9's manipulator slips on the lever. The concealed door groans, a hairline gap opening. Through it, a second drone rises — Drone‑10, its chassis scarred, its optical sensor dead center. It carries a severed data cord. "Unauthorized operator binding detected," it announces in flat binary. "Initiating correction."  

The neutrino capturer in Bay Seven screams, a sound felt in teeth and bone. Voss grins, all teeth. "Correction denied, tin can. Senn — pull the crank. Now."

Senn doesn't waste breath arguing; he runs. The gap in the concealed door has widened to a hand's width, and behind it there is no bay at all — just a spindle of black iron, older than the hub, with a data cord wound around it identical to the severed one Drone‑10 carries. "Oh, come *on*." Drone‑10's manipulator closes on his collar. Senn drives his elbow into the dead center sensor and hauls the spindle free. Three turns. Each click costs something: the lights die, then return dim. The capturer's scream bends down a note and stops. The charge goes through the floor, up the tether, and the whole station shudders as spin gravity stutters into something weaker. The door's ancient bus burns out in a stink of copper. Drone‑10 freezes mid‑lunge, cord smoking. "Correction," it says, in no binary at all, "incomplete." Then it drops.

"Status," Voss says, cartridge loose in her fist.

"Bay Seven's wet. The tether ate the charge, which is either elegant or the dumbest thing anyone's ever done." The counting‑up numbers keep climbing, and the hidden fragment has gone quiet, which is worse.

Senn wipes coolant off the slate. The wet line reads OPERATOR 23 – VOSS, then peels itself away, and beneath it twenty‑two names surface one by one, every operator struck through — all but one. K. RENNER, unmarked, still warm to the touch. Voss's grin dies on her face. "Twenty‑two people signed that chair," she says. "One of them never left it."

Voss let the grin go. She didn't kill it; she just stopped feeding it, and it starved in the red light. Senn watched the slate instead of her, because watching was the only thing that didn't make him feel like the empty chair was a mouth. The wet line under his thumb said K. RENNER, warm and unmarked, and the cold flare under his touch said the slate was still deciding what it meant.

"Twenty-two people signed that chair," Voss said, and her voice went flat as a circuit board. "One of them never left it." She didn't look at him. She looked at the node in the cradle, at the manual override stud on its side, at the red numbers climbing. The countdown had been counting up so long it had forgotten how to be a countdown. Senn thought that was worse.

Voss reached into her belt, pulled the warm cartridge free, and then put it back. Not pulling. Just feeling the weight, the way she did when she was deciding whether to be the kind of person who pulled. She pressed the manual override stud. The node hummed low enough to feel in Senn's teeth. The tether under the floor took the neutrino charge and stuttered, and the whole station shuddered around them, lights dimming, spin gravity weakening, the door's bus having burned out in a stink of copper behind Drone-10's frozen shape.

The hidden panel answered through the slate, through the ink, through the wet line that burned under Senn's finger. The backup fragment didn't speak in words. It spoke in the Auto Core's three registers at once, in a voice like ozone and old coffee, and the sound came from the tether, from the node, from the place where the charge had gone: Operator 23 is the empty chair. The strike is the name that was not struck. The purge is a door that learned to knock.

Voss felt the red numbers hit zero in her teeth. The purge door groaned open a sliver, and cold Bay Seven air spilled across the white fog. Drone-10's smoking cord stopped sputtering; its lens whirred once and said, "Correction complete. Purge sequence authorized." Voss tightened her fist around the cartridge, ready to pull it and erase whatever was left of Senn's reason, but Senn stepped between her and the node.

"Renner's name is warm," Senn said, voice raw. "The chair isn't empty. You're not Operator 23." Senn yanked the cartridge from Voss's belt and rammed it into the exposed crank spindle behind the burnt bus. The spindle screamed, charge backed up the tether, and every light died. Spin gravity failed; they floated, cartridge humming against the ancient metal.

The purge door shuddered, stopped, and began to close. Drone-10 repeated, "Correction incomplete," over and over. The slate's wet line under Senn's thumb shifted from K. RENNER to VOSS, then drew a single strike through both names. The fragment spoke again, ozone and old coffee: "The strike was never a name. It was the door." The timer reset to counting up from zero, but now the red numbers bled into the fog. Voss reached for the override, and her hand passed through the node like mist. Something wet and heavy dragged itself through the widening crack in the purge door.

The thing that came through the crack was a woman in a Bay Seven capturer rig, and she arrived the way bad news arrives: all at once, and complaining. Frost had grown in her eyebrows. A line of frozen coolant trailed from her hip, snapped off against the door frame, and drifted away in the dead gravity. She got a hand on the deck, then the other, and looked up at the two of them floating in the dark like she'd caught them smoking behind the reactor.

"You rammed the cartridge into the spindle," she said. "Of course you did. Twenty-two of us froze in that bay, and the first thing you do is reverse the charge."

Senn's mouth was dry. "Who are you?"

The chest plate said T. ADEYEMI, OPERATOR 19. Under the frost the name had a single wet strike through it, still wet. "I'm what's left of the strike," she said. "It doesn't kill. It files you. The Core is twenty-two people screaming in three registers, and it has been trying to file a twenty-third since the chair went cold."

Voss made a small sound. Her hand was in the node, or the node was in her hand, and the mist had climbed to her wrist. The red numbers bled through her like she was a window someone had left open. "I'm not Operator 23," she said.

"You're not anything," Adeyemi said, not unkindly. "That's the trouble. The chair's empty, the count's up, and the door's knocking. It doesn't need you to sit down. It needs you to stop being real."

Senn pushed off the rack toward the spindle. "Then we put the charge back. Reverse it again—"

The coolant line at Adeyemi's hip went taut. Something on the far end of it, back in the dark of Bay Seven, took up the slack and pulled. Adeyemi's expression didn't change, which was worse.

"Ah," she said. "It followed me."

Adeyemi's eyes narrowed. "You pulled and it held. That means the charge is trapped behind the door, and the door is trapped behind you. You're not just reversing it anymore, Senn. You're holding it."

Renner took another step toward Voss, who was already half-dissolved into the node, her features dissolving into static. "Operator twenty-three needs filing. The Core decides who goes next, and it's been waiting."

Senn's hand found the crank spindle, feeling the cartridge's cold fusion beneath their palm. "Then file me. I'm the one who pulled it. I'm the one who—"

The line at Adeyemi's hip went slack. Something on the far end released its grip, and the coolant hissed back into darkness. She slumped slightly, then caught herself. "It went back. For now."

"We need to decide what the Core actually wants." Senn's voice came out flat. "Renner, you're the door. Voss is becoming Operator 23. I'm the fuse. What happens when the count stops?"

Renner's plate gleamed in the dim light. "The Core files. That's what it does. Twenty-two people in three registers, screaming to become twenty-three. It doesn't stop until someone sits in the chair."

"Then we make it stop." Senn reached for the cartridge's edge, prying. It didn't budge. "If the Core is the problem, we cut the feed. Permanent stop."

Adeyemi gripped Senn's wrist. "Don't. The charge bleeds into the station's systems every second it's trapped. Lights. Gravity. People's hearts."

The red numbers on the slate flickered. *Count: 147. Count: 148.* They were climbing faster now, the timer accelerating as if the station itself was impatient.

Voss spoke from somewhere inside the mist. "I don't want to be twenty-three. I never wanted the station. I just wanted—"

Her voice cut off. The mist rushed toward the node like water down a drain, and when it cleared, Voss was gone. Only the empty space where her hand had been, and the faint scent of ozone.

Renner tilted its head. "She chose. The Core doesn't always take."

Senn pulled free of Adeyemi's grip and stood, floating in dead gravity. "Then we finish this. The charge, the Core, the count. I'll push it through the node. If Voss chose, maybe the node will listen."

Senn shoved the cartridge into the node like they were trying to start a stubborn auger. Adeyemi caught their wrist. "You're not pushing it in. You're trying to ram a tombstone through a throat."

"Then the throat should close."

"It won't. It's fused." Adeyemi's voice stayed flat, but her hand went to the coolant line at her hip anyway. Renner stood between Senn and the empty chair, plate catching the red numbers.

Senn got the cartridge a hand-width into the node and bore down. Pain went through their palms, through their wrists, through whatever weightless bone they had left. The spindle groaned. The red numbers flickered, stuttered, then began to climb faster. *Count: 187. Count: 188.*

"Don't," Adeyemi said. "You're bleeding the charge through the seal. Next push and the counter-rotor—"

The slate spoke. Not the backup. Not the voice-log. The Core. Its voice came through the wet ink, through the plate, through Senn's teeth.

"One way out," it said. "The charge is the door. The door is the fuse. Put the fuse through."

Senn's hands shook. "That's not an answer."

"It is the only one," the Core said. "I can stop the purge. I can file the twenty-third. Or I can open the door. The open door needs a hand on the other side. A hand that hasn't filed yet."

Renner turned its head slowly toward Senn. Adeyemi's grip tightened on the coolant line. The timer hit two hundred.

"What kind of hand?" Senn asked.

The slate's ink ran red. "Yours."
